result:
At the edge of every city there is a place where things begin to loosen.

Streetlights grow farther apart. Sidewalks become gravel. Buildings give way to warehouses, then fences, then fields nobody is quite responsible for. In these places, weeds reclaim the cracks with quiet confidence. Old signs point toward businesses that closed years ago. A train may pass at midnight, carrying containers full of objects whose destinations no one nearby will ever know.

I like these borders because they refuse to be impressive. They are not landmarks. No one takes postcards of a drainage ditch behind a shopping center, or of a half-empty parking lot glowing blue beneath a pharmacy sign. Yet they hold an honest kind of beauty: the beauty of things continuing without an audience.

A plastic bag catches on a branch and becomes, briefly, a flag. Rainwater gathers in a pothole and reflects a perfect upside-down sky. A cat slips beneath a rusted gate as though it has been entrusted with an important secret.

Perhaps most of life happens in such unnoticed intervals—not in grand arrivals or final departures, but in the long spaces between them. Coffee cooling on a desk. A song heard from another room. The moment before someone answers a question. The small decision to keep walking.

There is comfort in knowing that the world does not require every moment to mean something enormous. Some moments are simply allowed to exist: wind moving through tall grass, a distant engine, a window lit in an otherwise dark building.

And somehow, that is enough.
